title: Oak Creek, 2012
hook: six worshipers are killed at a Wisconsin gurdwara, and the sangat answers with prayer and open doors

segments.voice: Yesterday, after September 2001: Balbir Singh Sodhi, and a brother who told his story. Your line was know your neighbor. Today, another hard day, and an answer that drew strangers in. Go gently. Day three hundred twenty-one.

A Sunday morning in August, in Oak Creek, a suburb near Milwaukee, Wisconsin. At the gurdwara, the day starts early. Women are in the kitchen getting langar ready for the Sunday crowd. A few people are already sitting with the Guru Granth Sahib, and more families are on their way. An ordinary Sunday, the kind gurdwaras keep every week. Then a man walks in from the parking lot with a gun. Today: Oak Creek.
screen: `A SUNDAY IN AUGUST, WISCONSIN.` → `LANGAR BEING READIED.` → `A MAN FROM THE PARKING LOT.`

segments.voice: On the fifth of August, 2012, a gunman who held white supremacist views killed six people at the Sikh Temple of Wisconsin. The gurdwara's president, Satwant Singh Kaleka, tried to stop him and was killed. So were Paramjit Kaur, Prakash Singh, Sita Singh, Ranjit Singh and Suveg Singh. They had names. A granthi, Baba Punjab Singh, was badly wounded and died of his injuries years later. A police officer, Lieutenant Brian Murphy, was shot many times helping, and survived. The gunman killed himself. Now, what the sangat did next. They held Ardas for the dead. When the police handed the building back, they cleaned the hall. And they opened the doors. In the days and weeks after, the sangat welcomed neighbors, reporters, police officers and strangers, and fed them langar. Some of those visitors had never been inside a gurdwara, and they were handed a plate of food by the people who had just been attacked. In the years since, the community has marked the anniversary with a remembrance run named for chardi kala, rising spirits. And one more thread: Satwant Singh Kaleka's son, Pardeep, later became friends with a man who had once been a white supremacist himself. Together they started going into schools to talk about hate and how people leave it behind. None of this means the grief was small. It wasn't. But the sangat chose not to lock the door. In Sikh teaching, the sangat, the holy company, is where the Guru is found. When the sangat was hurt, it stayed together, and it stayed open. That's the line: the doors stayed open.
screen: `AUGUST 5, 2012: SIX KILLED.` · `THEY HAD NAMES.` · `ARDAS, AND LANGAR FOR STRANGERS.` · `A SON, AND A FORMER ENEMY.` · then, large: `THE DOORS STAYED OPEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a grieving community. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the families of Oak Creek, and then any community you know that is grieving right now, near or far. Picture their hall, their kitchen, their people sitting close together. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If you don't, simply wish them comfort and strength, and stay with them in the quiet for a while. The bell holds the time.
Oak Creek. In 2012, six worshipers were killed at a Wisconsin gurdwara, and the sangat answered with Ardas, langar and open doors.
Your line: the doors stayed open. Today, after something hurts you, choose one small way to stay open instead of closing up: a reply, a visit, a kind word. Day three hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Each August the Oak Creek sangat remembers those killed with Ardas, kirtan and a community run named for chardi kala, and the gurdwara continues to welcome neighbors to langar.

fork.setup: your gurdwara has just been attacked, and strangers and reporters are gathering outside. what does the Oak Creek sangat do?
options: lock the doors and keep outsiders away.
hold Ardas and open the doors, with langar.
move to a new building far away.
fork.reveal: they held Ardas for the dead, cleaned the hall, and fed everyone who came, including people who had never been inside a gurdwara.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sangat, the holy company; Sikhs say the Guru is found where the sangat gathers.

trapdoor: what you thought: after an attack, a community closes its doors.
what it means: the Oak Creek sangat stayed together, stayed open, and fed strangers.
what a scholar hears: after the August 5, 2012 attack, Sikh groups pressed the FBI to count anti-Sikh hate crimes separately, and it began doing so in 2015.

notes: The six names are given as widely reported (Satwant Singh Kaleka, Paramjit Kaur, Prakash Singh, Sita Singh, Ranjit Singh, Suveg Singh Khattra); Baba Punjab Singh died in 2020. Keeper and, ideally, the Oak Creek community should confirm spellings and whether names should be read.
The gunman is deliberately not named.

The annual run is described as 'the Chardi Kala run' (reported as the Chardi Kala 6K); confirm its exact name and that it is still held. The sequence 'cleaned the hall, held Ardas, opened the doors' compresses several days during which the building was a crime scene; confirm timing.
The FBI began recording anti-Sikh hate crimes as a separate category in 2015 (trapdoor); confirm.
Pardeep Kaleka's work with Arno Michaelis (Serve2Unite) is described without names for the second man; confirm.
